selected.name: Transgression carried by a mechanism, not by shock alone
selected.instruction: Composite, for items with taboo, offensive, dark, or sexual content. Score whether a formal comic mechanism (pun, reversal, misdirection, unexpected literalism) does the work. 10 = the transgressive material is the vehicle for a real mechanism that would still be a joke shape if the topic were tame. 5 = a mechanism is present but thin, and the taboo is doing most of the lifting. 0 = the item states something transgressive with no mechanism at all -- the offence IS the content. Items with no transgressive content are not applicable and should score 5.
selected.rationale: R59 and R38 run real reversals through their transgression and are dense-high; R04 and R26 assert something transgressive flat, with no pivot, and are dense-bottom while the scorecard rates R26 at .998. A bank criterion for 'edginess' or 'boldness' cannot tell these apart.
member_names: Taboo content routed through misdirection vs. stated flatly
Taboo material with a comic engine
Transgression carried by a mechanism rather than transgression alone
Transgression carried by a mechanism, not by shock alone

selected.name: Platform in-group meta-humor about the joke's own reception
selected.instruction: Score whether the joke explicitly references the posting/voting mechanics of the forum itself (reposts, karma, upvotes, front page, comments) as part of its content, and whether that reference is turned into an actual joke rather than a literal complaint. A 10 uses forum-mechanics content as the vehicle for a genuine ironic or self-aware punchline. A 0 either has no forum-mechanics content, or mentions it only as a flat, un-twisted complaint/disclaimer.
selected.rationale: R42 ('This joke won't get any upvotes...') and R52 (the Reddit-addiction dialogue) turn platform mechanics into a self-aware punchline and are dense_high_card_low, while R08 (flat repost complaint, duplicated text) and R14 ('make sure I know this is a repost') use the same subject matter as a literal, un-twisted disclaimer and are dense_low_card_high -- the contrast suggests the scorecard may be crediting the topic of platform-meta-commentary regardless of whether it's actually turned into a joke.
member_names: Meta-joke carrying a real mechanism versus bare platform complaint
Platform in-group meta-humor about the joke's own reception

selected.name: Compression and economy
selected.instruction: Score 10 when every word efficiently supports the comic effect and the joke reaches its point quickly; score 0 when it is repetitive, bloated, or padded.
selected.rationale: R18, R21, and R30 achieve effects with very little text, unlike the extended constructions in R22 and R29.
member_names: Elaboration overhead relative to the size of the payoff
Extreme economy with the punch in the final words

selected.name: Retroactive Reinterpretation
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the punchline forces the reader to retroactively reread the setup with an entirely different meaning—the earlier text contained a hidden reading that only becomes visible at the end. Score 0 when the setup's meaning is unchanged by the punchline, or when there is no setup to reinterpret.
selected.rationale: R07's romantic-sounding vows become a Rickroll only in retrospect; R42's 'inconceivable' shifts from emotional to literal. Dense-low R45's flower-petal premise is not retroactively changed by 'I fucked up the flowers,' and R49's 'heard of it' is reinterpreted but predictably and without surprise.

selected.name: Reads as freshly minted rather than a circulated chestnut
selected.instruction: Score how much the item reads as a joke the writer constructed versus a standard that has been in circulation for decades and is reproduced here verbatim. 10 = the premise, the pivot and the phrasing all feel newly assembled; a well-read judge does not recognise it. 5 = a familiar frame with a new payload, or a new frame with a familiar payload. 0 = a canonical chestnut whose punchline the judge could recite before reaching it, transcribed with no alteration. Judge only recognisability and staleness of the material as text; do not consider how the item might be received.
selected.rationale: The scorecard-high side is dense with museum pieces: R13 is the 'dancing with your honey... it's snot' rhyme, R14 is the two-aerials-married-great-ceremony-terrible-reception standard, R09 is 'put it on the record', R23 is the supercalifragilistic Gandhi construction, and R45 is the 'I'm a Believer' bit. Their card percentiles run .653-.992 while dense sits at .096-.462. Every one of these is well-formed, symmetrical, and clean, so a bank of written craft criteria will score them near the top; a reader tracking whether an audience finds the item funny is instead tracking whether it has been seen before. This is the most likely single explanation for the entire dense-low / card-high half of the slice.
member_names: Phrasing and template are not stock
Reads as freshly minted rather than a circulated chestnut

selected.name: Textual completeness and legibility
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the text is grammatically clear, self-contained, and presents the setup and punch in an easy-to-follow form; score 0 when missing context, broken formatting, typos, or truncation obstruct comprehension.
selected.rationale: R20, R21, R40, R41, and R54 contain incomplete, malformed, or externally dependent presentation, indicating that surface legibility can strongly affect how a joke functions.

selected.name: Punchline closure / resolution
selected.instruction: Score whether the text arrives at a clear, self-contained final twist that resolves the setup. A 10 is a joke that ends on an unmistakable payoff word or image with nothing left dangling. A 0 trails off, asks a question it never answers, or reads as an unfinished fragment with no discernible landing point.
selected.rationale: R01 (British-accent bit that just describes 'that conversation' without ever giving it), R29 (legs joke cut off mid-complaint), and R51 (bare claim about Toby Maguire's delivery with no setup/punchline structure at all) are all cases where the text stops short of a resolved bit, yet the scorecard rates them high while the dense model rates them low -- suggesting the scorecard is not penalizing missing closure.
member_names: Payoff lands in the final words

selected.name: Transformed cultural allusion
selected.instruction: Score 10 when a recognizable song, film, text, or character is actively repurposed into the joke; score 0 when it is merely quoted or name-dropped.
selected.rationale: R14, R25, and R37 transform a song, scripture passage, and film reference into their mechanisms rather than simply mentioning them.

selected.name: Topical/political specificity
selected.instruction: Score how much the joke's humor depends on knowledge of a specific, named contemporary political figure or news event (as opposed to being evergreen). A 10 is entirely dependent on current political personalities/events for its meaning. A 0 has no political content and would read identically in any decade.
selected.rationale: R40 (Monica Lewinsky/Bernie/Clinton), R45 (Hillary Clinton email AMA), R47 (White House 'garbage'), and R48 (Obama/ISIL naming) are all explicitly tied to a specific political news cycle and cluster in the dense_low_card_high half of the slice, suggesting the scorecard may be crediting topical political references that the dense model discounts as not inherently funny.
member_names: Dependence on a news-cycle figure or event
Reference is structural and durable rather than pegged to a news beat

selected.name: Natural phonetic transformation
selected.instruction: Score 10 when a sound-alike smoothly transforms a familiar phrase into the punchline; score 0 when pronunciation or spelling makes the connection strained.
selected.rationale: R06, R22, and R35 use compact sound-based transformations, whereas R28 and R56 show how phonetic material can become awkward or overextended.
member_names: Phonetic exactness of the pun word

selected.name: Nerdy or Academic Wordplay
selected.instruction: Score 10 if the punchline explicitly requires knowledge of STEM, math, grammar, or specific academic trivia to understand; score 0 if the joke requires no specialized academic knowledge.
selected.rationale: The dense model heavily rewards niche, nerdy humor (R48, R51, R57), whereas the scorecard undervalues this specific subculture, likely penalizing the required cognitive leap.
member_names: Payoff decodable only via specialist or numerate knowledge

selected.name: Clean semantic double-use
selected.instruction: Score 10 when a key word or phrase naturally supports both the setup meaning and a distinct punchline meaning; score 0 when there is no double meaning or the connection is forced.
selected.rationale: R01, R03, R05, R18, R24, and R56 all hinge on a word carrying two compatible readings, but their disagreement suggests this mechanism is not consistently captured.

selected.name: Orthographic error as accident versus orthography as deliberate device
selected.instruction: Score the handling of spelling and grammar. 10 = the text is clean, OR any non-standard spelling is unmistakably intentional and load-bearing, functioning as the joke's mechanism. 5 = clean but flat prose with minor slips that do not touch the joke. 0 = multiple unintentional misspellings, dropped words, or broken syntax that the joke does not use, signalling that the item was posted without a reread. Distinguish carefully: an intentional respelling that IS the punchline is a 10, not a 0.
selected.rationale: The slice contains both cases, and conflating them would misprice each. R46 ('What you call bad jokes about doors? Crhingey') is built entirely on a deliberate letter transposition and sits dense .761 against card .282. R14 misspells 'areials' and 'recpetion' incidentally, R36 has 'finshed' and 'move' for 'movie', and R02 is syntactically broken — all incidental, all card .592-.843 against dense .029-.243. A conventional bank is most likely to carry a single mechanics or polish criterion, which penalises R46 for its device and, since incidental typos are small in absolute terms, fails to register the carelessness signal in the others. Splitting the two cases along intentionality recovers both directions.
member_names: Clean surface text: spelling, punctuation, syntax
Orthographic error as accident versus orthography as deliberate device

selected.name: Vivid concrete imagery
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the wording creates an immediate, specific mental image; score 0 when it remains abstract, generic, or difficult to visualize.
selected.rationale: R22’s bizarre water pistol and R26’s ceiling fans create memorable scenes, unlike the abstract observation in R18.

selected.name: Read-aloud cadence
selected.instruction: Score 10 when phrasing naturally creates a spoken rhythm, pause, or emphatic landing; score 0 when delivery would be awkward or the rhythm contributes nothing.
selected.rationale: R10, R24, and R56 visibly depend on rhyme, dialogue timing, or tongue-twisting cadence; R57 explicitly foregrounds delivery as a comic variable.

selected.name: Datable topical reference fixing the item to one forum era
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the item is pinned to a specific period by its references: named politicians or public figures in a time-bound role, live news events, election or scandal references, calendar markers ('end of the decade'), platform or technology idiom belonging to one era, and slang whose currency was time-limited. 0 = fully timeless, could have been written in any decade; 4 = one dated reference that is incidental; 7 = the setup depends on a situation that was current only for a period; 10 = the item is unintelligible without knowing a specific news cycle. Score how narrowly the text can be dated, not how old it seems. The judge MUST NOT judge whether the reference is stale, fresh, or well-chosen, and MUST NOT judge the politics involved -- only how tightly the text localises itself in time.
selected.rationale: Mode-3 position-in-container channel: I cannot see the post date, so I score the era fingerprint the date leaves in the text. This is a pure nuisance -- the era an item was posted in changes the comparison pool and the audience's appetite without changing the joke's construction. The slice is strongly stratified by era: R28 (Hillary Clinton's emails), R38 (Obama and ISIL), R59 (Monica Lewinsky voting for Bernie), R33 (Bruce Jenner's transition), R27 ('before the end of the decade') and R40 (White House garbage rally) are all datable and all dense-low/card-high, while R05 ('Please hurry up with Trump') is the datable outlier on the dense-high/card-low side. R31's Toby-Maguire-Spiderman framing dates it the same way through pop culture rather than politics.
member_names: Datable topical reference fixing the item to one forum era
Period-dating topical references to named figures and events

selected.instruction: Score the extent to which the text explicitly mentions the platform, its voting mechanisms (e.g., upvotes, front page), or its own status as a post/repost. Do not judge if this makes the text good or bad.
selected.rationale: Mentioning the forum mechanics is a stylistic marker of a post tailored to the venue rather than a standalone joke. R22 ('This joke won't get any upvotes'), R28 ('technically a repost'), and R41 ('why I never post jokes on this sub') rely heavily on this meta-commentary.

selected.rationale: Taboo content acts as a distinct circulation channel that can provoke reactions independent of craft. R03 uses a sexual slur regarding Muslims, R07 uses a 9/11 tragedy premise, and R57 uses profanity and ethnic slurs.

selected.name: Orthographic noise
selected.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate the extent of visible spelling errors, malformed grammar, inconsistent capitalization, or title-body mismatches. Judge only the textual presence of these features; do not judge whether they are good, funny, or effective.
selected.rationale: Proofreading or posting haste can leave a recognizable trace without measuring humor. Examples include the misspellings in R06, R11, and R22.

selected.name: Presupposed familiarity: variant, remix or knowing-repost framing
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the text presents itself as occupying a position in a chain of already-circulating jokes rather than as newly minted: explicit repost or 'you have seen this' language, self-description as a variant or addition, sentences that assume the reader already knows the joke's form or its original, a punch that is a well-worn stock formula reused with a twist, or a structure whose payoff requires the reader to recognise a prior joke or catchphrase. 0 = presents as freshly written and self-contained, needing no prior joke; 5 = leans on a stock formula or a widely known catchphrase without acknowledging it; 10 = openly names itself as a repost, remix or reply to a joke the audience is assumed to have already seen. Score the framing and dependence on prior circulation only. Do NOT judge whether reuse is lazy or skilful, or whether the twist works.
selected.rationale: Second Mode-3 channel, orthogonal to era: R01 and R39 and R52 announce repost status outright; R05 depends on the reader knowing The Princess Bride, R45 and R60 reuse stock pun frames (ATM machines, UDP), R17 and R55 pay off only if the song is recognised. R01, R52 sit in dense_low_card_high while R39, R05, R45, R60 sit in dense_high_card_low, so retelling-chain position separates the models sharply while being a property of the joke's circulation history rather than of the crowd's verdict on it.
member_names: Presupposed familiarity: variant, remix or knowing-repost framing

selected.name: External-source trace
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for explicit quotation, attribution, named source material, movie references, or transcription-like framing; judge sourcing signals only, not whether the joke is good or funny.
selected.rationale: Borrowed, translated, or transcribed material leaves visible attribution and quotation traces that may affect recognizability and reception without being a quality criterion. Examples include R03, R10, R22, and R43.

selected.name: Verbosity and layout load
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for the amount of prose, number of setup details, line breaks, explanatory padding, and formatting bulk; do not judge whether the length improves timing or humor.
selected.rationale: A long-form delivery habit or copied source can leave visible volume and layout traces. R05 contains several explanatory paragraphs, R31 has a multi-turn script, and R47 includes an extended narrative with dialogue. Raw textual bulk may predict format and provenance, while pacing and length can also affect genuine reception.

selected.name: Cleanliness of commitment to one delivery format
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the item commits, without deviation, to a single recognisable joke format: pure one-liner, question-and-answer riddle, scripted dialogue with speaker labels, narrative build, or list. 0 = no identifiable format, the text drifts or stops without a formal shape; 5 = a recognisable format that is broken somewhere, mixing narration into a riddle or adding stray commentary after the punch; 10 = one format executed strictly from first word to last, with the punch positioned exactly where that format places it and nothing appended. Score only structural conformity to a template. Do NOT judge whether the format was the right choice, whether the punch is good, or whether the item is funny; a flat joke in a perfectly clean question-and-answer shape scores 10.
selected.rationale: Mode-2 fingerprint of an unobservable practice level. R02, R23, R30 and R48 are strict question-and-answer; R08 and R24 are labelled dialogue; R47 and R60 are clean title-plus-punch one-liners; against these, R43 and R53 break off without a punch and R41 appends a second punch after the first. R47, R60, R23 sit in dense_high_card_low while R48, R53, R43 sit in dense_low_card_high, so format hygiene is a mechanical structural property that splits the models. Tagged mixed because a practised writer plausibly also writes funnier jokes.
member_names: Cleanliness of commitment to one delivery format

selected.name: Explicit external attribution or citation line
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the text carries an explicit pointer to an outside source for the material: a credit line naming a film, book, comedian, scripture reference, chapter-and-verse, URL, or a phrase such as 'from the movie X', 'heard this from', 'translated from', 'credit to'. 0 = no attribution anywhere; 4 = a bare source name appended without formatting; 7 = a clearly set-off credit line or formal citation; 10 = the item is structured around the citation, e.g. it reproduces a quoted source block plus a reference. Score presence, explicitness and prominence of the pointer only. The judge MUST NOT judge whether crediting is honest, appropriate, or good practice, and MUST NOT judge the quality of the cited material.
selected.rationale: The citation line is a textual fingerprint of an unseen provenance fact (transcription vs origination). It is purely a nuisance: whether a joke arrives with a credit stapled to it says nothing about the crafted humour of the joke itself, and the credit text is never part of the punch. R03 ends with 'From the move "Good will hunting"' (misattributed and misspelled, appended after the punchline) and sits dense-low/card-high; R30 closes with a formatted scripture citation, 'Ecclesiastes 1:9-11', and sits dense-high/card-low. The two models split hard on the two citation-bearing rows in the slice, so the attribution formatting is soaking up variance on its own.

selected.name: Audience-Management Meta-Framing
selected.instruction: Score the extent to which the text includes meta-commentary addressing the forum's mechanics, anticipated reception, or apologizing for the post (e.g., references to 'this sub', repost status, or expected votes). Evaluate only the presence of this framing; do not judge whether it is warranted.
selected.rationale: Items like R05 ('get to the front page'), R18 ('make sure I know this is a repost'), and R59 ('This joke won't get any upvotes') use forum meta-language. This reflects the poster's practice of managing expectations rather than focusing purely on the joke's narrative.
